# Complex Roots of Unity are Vertices of a Regular Polygon Inscribed in a Circle

## Statement

Let $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $n \ge 3$, and let
$$U_n \;=\; \bigl\{\, e^{2 i k \pi / n} \;:\; k \in \mathbb{N}_n \,\bigr\},\qquad \mathbb{N}_n = \{0,1,\dots ,n-1\},$$
be the set of $n$th roots of unity, plotted in the complex plane.

**Theorem.** $U_n$ is exactly the solution set of $z^n = 1$ in $\mathbb{C}$; it consists of $n$ distinct points; and these points are precisely the vertices of a regular $n$-sided polygon $P$ such that

1. $P$ is circumscribed by the unit circle centred at $\left(0,0\right)$ — that is, all $n$ vertices lie on that circle, and it is the unique circle through them; and
2. one of the vertices is the point $\left(1,0\right)$.

Moreover each side of $P$ has length $2\sin\frac{\pi}{n}$, each interior angle equals $\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}$, and $P$ is convex.

## 0. Conventions

We identify $\mathbb{C}$ with the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ via $x+iy \leftrightarrow \left(x,y\right)$. Under this identification the Euclidean distance between points $z,w$ is $\left|z-w\right|$, and the Euclidean inner product of $z,w$ viewed as vectors is $\langle z,w\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\bigl(z\overline{w}\bigr)$; in particular, for a fixed unit vector $m$ the map $z \mapsto \operatorname{Re}(z\overline m)$ is a non-zero $\mathbb{R}$-linear functional on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

For $u,v,w \in \mathbb{C}$ with $u \ne v$ and $w \ne v$, the (unsigned) **angle** at $v$ is
$$\angle\,u\,v\,w \;=\; \arccos \frac{\operatorname{Re}\bigl((u-v)\overline{(w-v)}\bigr)}{\left|u-v\right|\,\left|w-v\right|} \;\in\;[0,\pi].$$

A **polygon** $v_0v_1\cdots v_{m-1}v_0$ ($m \ge 3$, vertices pairwise distinct) is the closed polygonal curve $\Pi = \bigcup_{i} [v_i,v_{i+1}]$ (indices mod $m$) subject to: it is **simple**, i.e. two non-adjacent edges are disjoint and two adjacent edges meet exactly in their common endpoint; and no vertex angle $\angle v_{i-1}v_iv_{i+1}$ equals $\pi$, so that each $v_i$ really is a corner. Its **sides** are the segments $[v_i,v_{i+1}]$. By the Jordan curve theorem for polygons, $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \Pi$ has exactly two connected components, one bounded and one unbounded; the bounded one is the **interior** $\operatorname{Int}\Pi$ of the polygon.

The **interior angle** of $\Pi$ at the vertex $v_i$ is the angular measure of the set
$$D_i \;=\; \bigl\{\, d \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \left|d\right| = 1,\ v_i + t d \in \operatorname{Int}\Pi \text{ for all sufficiently small } t>0 \,\bigr\},$$
i.e. the arclength of $D_i$ regarded as a subset of the unit circle. (For the usual polygons this is the familiar interior angle: the opening of the interior region between the two edges at $v_i$.)

A polygon is **equilateral** if all sides have the same length; **equiangular** if all interior angles are equal; **regular** if it is both. It is **convex** if its interior is a convex set. A circle is **circumscribed around** a polygon if every vertex lies on that circle.

We use freely the standard facts $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$, $\left|e^{i\theta}\right| = 1$, $e^{i\theta}e^{i\varphi} = e^{i(\theta+\varphi)}$, $\overline{e^{i\theta}} = e^{-i\theta}$, and
$$e^{i\theta} = 1 \iff \theta \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}. \tag{$\ast$}$$

Throughout, $n \ge 3$ is fixed and we write
$$\omega = e^{2i\pi/n},\qquad z_j = \omega^{\,j} = e^{2ij\pi/n}\ (j \in \mathbb{Z}),\qquad \alpha = \pi - \frac{2\pi}{n} = \frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}.$$
Since $n\ge 3$ we have $0 < \frac{2\pi}{n} \le \frac{2\pi}{3} < \pi$, hence
$$0 \;<\; \frac{\pi}{3} \;\le\; \alpha \;<\; \pi. \tag{0.1}$$

## 1. The points $z_j$

**(1.1) $z_j$ depends only on $j \bmod n$, and $U_n = \{z_0,z_1,\dots ,z_{n-1}\}$.**
Indeed $\omega^{\,n} = e^{2i\pi} = 1$ by $(\ast)$, so $z_{j+n} = z_j\omega^{\,n} = z_j$. The second assertion is the definition of $U_n$.

**(1.2) $\left|z_j\right| = 1$ for all $j$.** Immediate from $\left|e^{i\theta}\right| = 1$. So every element of $U_n$ lies on the unit circle centred at $0$.

**(1.3) $z_0 = 1$**, i.e. the point $\left(1,0\right)$ belongs to $U_n$.

**(1.4) $z_0,\dots ,z_{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct; hence $\#\left(U_n\right) = n$.**
Suppose $z_p = z_q$ with $0 \le p < q \le n-1$. Dividing, $\omega^{\,q-p} = 1$, i.e. $e^{2i(q-p)\pi/n} = 1$, so by $(\ast)$ we get $\frac{2(q-p)\pi}{n} \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $n \mid (q-p)$. But $0 < q-p \le n-1 < n$: contradiction.

**(1.5) $U_n = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : z^n = 1\}$.**
If $z = z_j$ then $z^n = \omega^{\,jn} = e^{2ij\pi} = 1$ by $(\ast)$. Conversely suppose $z^n = 1$. Then $\left|z\right|^n = \left|z^n\right| = 1$ with $\left|z\right|$ a positive real, so $\left|z\right| = 1$ and $z = e^{i\theta}$ for a (unique) $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$. From $e^{in\theta} = z^n = 1$ and $(\ast)$ we get $n\theta = 2k\pi$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $\theta = \frac{2k\pi}{n}$; and $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$ forces $0 \le k \le n-1$. Hence $z = z_k \in U_n$.

Thus the hypothesis "$z^n = 1$" of the statement describes exactly the elements of $U_n$, so nothing is lost by working with $U_n$.

**(1.6) Side length.** For all $j$, using (1.2),
$$\left|z_{j+1}-z_j\right| \;=\; \left|z_j\right|\,\left|\omega - 1\right| \;=\; \left|\omega-1\right|,$$
and
$$\left|\omega-1\right|^2 = \Bigl(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{n}-1\Bigr)^2 + \sin^2\tfrac{2\pi}{n} = 2 - 2\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{n} = 4\sin^2\tfrac{\pi}{n},$$
by $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$ and $1-\cos 2t = 2\sin^2 t$. Since $0 < \frac{\pi}{n} \le \frac{\pi}{3} < \pi$ we have $\sin\frac{\pi}{n} > 0$, so
$$s \;:=\; \left|z_{j+1}-z_j\right| \;=\; 2\sin\frac{\pi}{n} \;>\; 0 \qquad\text{for every } j. \tag{1.6.1}$$

## 2. The curve $P$ and the key separation lemma

For $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ put
$$E_k \;=\; [z_k,z_{k+1}] \;=\; \{(1-t)z_k + tz_{k+1} : t \in [0,1]\},\qquad P \;=\; \bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}E_k ,$$
so that $P$ is the closed polygonal curve $z_0z_1\cdots z_{n-1}z_0$. By (1.1), $E_k$ depends only on $k \bmod n$; by (1.6.1) each $E_k$ is a non-degenerate segment.

Put
$$m_k \;=\; e^{(2k+1)i\pi/n},\qquad f_k(z) \;=\; \operatorname{Re}\bigl(z\overline{m_k}\bigr),\qquad c \;=\; \cos\frac{\pi}{n}.$$
Each $f_k$ is a non-zero $\mathbb{R}$-linear functional (inner product with the unit vector $m_k$), so
$$L_k = \{z : f_k(z) = c\},\qquad H_k = \{z: f_k(z)\le c\}$$
are a straight line and a closed half-plane, with $\partial H_k = L_k$ and $\operatorname{int}H_k = \{z: f_k(z)<c\}$.

**Lemma 1 (Separation).** For all $j,k \in \mathbb{Z}$,
$$f_k(z_j) \;=\; \cos\frac{(2j-2k-1)\pi}{n},$$
and
$$f_k(z_j) = c \ \text{ if } j \equiv k \text{ or } j \equiv k+1 \ (\bmod\ n),\qquad f_k(z_j) < c \ \text{ otherwise.}$$
Consequently: $L_k$ is exactly the line through $z_k$ and $z_{k+1}$; $E_k \subseteq L_k$; every $z_j$ lies in $H_k$; and the only $z_j$ on $L_k$ are $z_k$ and $z_{k+1}$.

*Proof.* First,
$$f_k(z_j) = \operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e^{2ij\pi/n}\,e^{-(2k+1)i\pi/n}\Bigr) = \operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e^{i(2j-2k-1)\pi/n}\Bigr) = \cos\frac{(2j-2k-1)\pi}{n}.$$
Replacing $j$ by $j+n$ increases the argument by exactly $2\pi$, so the value depends only on $j \bmod n$, consistently with (1.1). Let $d \in \{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}$ with $d \equiv j-k \pmod n$; then $f_k(z_j) = \cos\frac{(2d-1)\pi}{n}$.

For $d = 0$ this is $\cos\bigl(-\frac\pi n\bigr) = c$, and for $d = 1$ it is $\cos\frac\pi n = c$; these are exactly the cases $j\equiv k$ and $j \equiv k+1$.

Now let $2 \le d \le n-1$ (such $d$ exist only when $n\ge 3$) and set $t = \frac{(2d-1)\pi}{n}$. Then
$$\frac{3\pi}{n} \;\le\; t \;\le\; \frac{(2n-3)\pi}{n} \;=\; 2\pi - \frac{3\pi}{n},$$
and these bounds are consistent since $3 \le 2n-3$ for $n \ge 3$. In particular
$$\frac{\pi}{n} \;<\; t \;<\; 2\pi - \frac{\pi}{n},\qquad 0<t<2\pi .$$
We show $\cos t < c$, distinguishing two exhaustive cases.
* If $\frac\pi n < t \le \pi$: $\cos$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ and $0 < \frac\pi n < t \le \pi$, so $\cos t < \cos\frac\pi n = c$.
* If $\pi < t < 2\pi - \frac\pi n$: $\cos$ is strictly increasing on $[\pi,2\pi]$ and $\pi \le t < 2\pi-\frac\pi n \le 2\pi$, so $\cos t < \cos\bigl(2\pi - \frac\pi n\bigr) = \cos\frac\pi n = c$.

Hence $f_k(z_j) < c$ whenever $j \not\equiv k, k+1 \pmod n$, which proves the displayed dichotomy.

Finally, $z_k,z_{k+1} \in L_k$ and $z_k \ne z_{k+1}$ by (1.6.1); since two distinct points lie on a unique line, $L_k$ is *the* line through $z_k$ and $z_{k+1}$, and $E_k \subseteq L_k$ because $L_k$ is convex. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary 2.** $H_k$ is convex and contains every $z_j$; hence $H_k \supseteq P$ and $H_k \supseteq C$, where
$$C \;:=\; \operatorname{conv}\{z_0,\dots ,z_{n-1}\}$$
is the (compact, convex) convex hull of $U_n$. In particular $C \subseteq \bigcap_{k=0}^{n-1}H_k$.

## 3. $P$ is a simple closed polygon with vertex set $U_n$

**Proposition 3.** Let $j,k \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $j \not\equiv k \pmod n$. Then
$$E_j \cap E_k \;=\;
\begin{cases}
\{z_{k+1}\} & \text{if } j \equiv k+1 \pmod n,\\
\{z_k\} & \text{if } j \equiv k-1 \pmod n,\\
\varnothing & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}$$
(For $n\ge 3$ the congruences $j\equiv k+1$ and $j \equiv k-1$ cannot hold simultaneously, since that would force $n \mid 2$; so the three cases are mutually exclusive.) Consequently $P$ is a simple closed polygonal curve.

*Proof.* Let $p \in E_j \cap E_k$. Write $p = (1-t)z_j + tz_{j+1}$ with $t \in [0,1]$. Since $p \in E_k \subseteq L_k$ (Lemma 1) and $f_k$ is linear,
$$(1-t)f_k(z_j) + t\,f_k(z_{j+1}) \;=\; f_k(p) \;=\; c. \tag{3.1}$$
By Lemma 1, $f_k(z_j)\le c$ and $f_k(z_{j+1}) \le c$. We consider the three possible cases for $t$.

*Case $0<t<1$.* Then (3.1) writes $c$ as a strict convex combination of two numbers that are both $\le c$; this forces $f_k(z_j) = f_k(z_{j+1}) = c$. By Lemma 1, $j\equiv k$ or $j\equiv k+1$; since $j\not\equiv k$ we get $j \equiv k+1$. Also $j+1 \equiv k$ or $j+1\equiv k+1$; substituting $j\equiv k+1$ gives $k+2 \equiv k$ or $k+2\equiv k+1$, i.e. $n \mid 2$ or $n\mid 1$ — impossible for $n \ge 3$. So this case does not occur.

*Case $t = 0$.* Then $p = z_j$ and $f_k(z_j) = c$, so by Lemma 1 $j\equiv k$ or $j\equiv k+1$; as $j \not\equiv k$, we get $j \equiv k+1$ and $p = z_j = z_{k+1}$.

*Case $t=1$.* Then $p = z_{j+1}$ and $f_k(z_{j+1}) = c$, so $j+1\equiv k$ or $j+1 \equiv k+1$; the latter gives $j \equiv k$, excluded; hence $j \equiv k-1$ and $p = z_{j+1} = z_k$.

Therefore: if $j\not\equiv k\pm 1 \pmod n$ then $E_j\cap E_k = \varnothing$; if $j \equiv k+1$ then $E_j \cap E_k \subseteq \{z_{k+1}\}$, and since $z_{k+1}$ does lie in both segments, $E_j\cap E_k = \{z_{k+1}\}$; symmetrically if $j\equiv k-1$ then $E_j \cap E_k = \{z_k\}$.

In the closed curve $z_0z_1\cdots z_{n-1}z_0$ the edges adjacent to $E_k$ are exactly $E_{k\pm1}$. So non-adjacent edges are disjoint, and adjacent edges meet exactly in their common vertex. Together with (1.4) (the $n$ vertices are distinct) this says that $P$ is a simple closed polygonal curve. $\blacksquare$

**Proposition 4 (no straight corners).** For every $k$, the points $z_k,z_{k+1},z_{k+2}$ are pairwise distinct and not collinear.

*Proof.* Since $n\ge 3$, the integers $k,k+1,k+2$ are pairwise incongruent mod $n$, so the three points are distinct by (1.1) and (1.4). All three lie on the unit circle by (1.2). A straight line meets a circle in at most two points: parametrising the line as $q + \tau e$ ($\left|e\right| = 1$, $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$) and substituting into $\left|z\right|^2 = 1$ gives $\tau^2 + 2\tau\operatorname{Re}(q\bar e) + \left|q\right|^2 - 1 = 0$, a quadratic with leading coefficient $1 \ne 0$, hence at most two roots $\tau$. Therefore the three points are not collinear. $\blacksquare$

By Propositions 3 and 4 (the latter giving $\angle z_kz_{k+1}z_{k+2} \ne \pi$, since collinearity is necessary for an angle of $\pi$), $P$ is a polygon in the sense of §0, with $n$ sides and with vertex set $\{z_0,\dots ,z_{n-1}\} = U_n$.

## 4. $P$ is equilateral

By (1.6.1) every side of $P$ has length $\left|z_{k+1}-z_k\right| = 2\sin\frac\pi n$, independently of $k$. Hence $P$ is equilateral with side length $2\sin\frac\pi n$. $\blacksquare$

## 5. The edge vectors at a vertex, and the vertex angle

Fix $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ and put
$$v = z_{k+1},\qquad a = z_k - v,\qquad b = z_{k+2}-v .$$

**Lemma 5.** $b = -\omega\,a = e^{-i\alpha}a$, and $\left|a\right| = \left|b\right| = s = 2\sin\frac\pi n > 0$. Consequently
$$\angle\,z_k\,z_{k+1}\,z_{k+2} \;=\; \alpha \;=\; \frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}.$$

*Proof.* We compute
$$a = z_k - z_k\omega = z_k(1-\omega), \qquad b = z_k\omega^2 - z_k\omega = z_k\,\omega\,(\omega-1) = -\omega\cdot z_k(1-\omega) = -\omega\,a .$$
Next,
$$-\omega = -e^{2i\pi/n} = e^{i\pi}e^{2i\pi/n} = e^{i(\pi + 2\pi/n)} = e^{i(2\pi/n-\pi)}\;=\;e^{-i(\pi - 2\pi/n)} \;=\; e^{-i\alpha},$$
where the middle equality holds because the two exponents differ by $2\pi$. Hence $b = e^{-i\alpha}a$, and $\left|b\right| = \left|e^{-i\alpha}\right|\left|a\right| = \left|a\right|$, which equals $s>0$ by (1.6.1).

For the angle: with $u = z_k$, $w = z_{k+2}$ we have $u - v = a \ne 0$ and $w-v = b = e^{-i\alpha}a \ne 0$, so
$$(u-v)\overline{(w-v)} \;=\; a\,\overline{e^{-i\alpha}a} \;=\; e^{i\alpha}\,a\overline a \;=\; e^{i\alpha}\left|a\right|^2 ,$$
whence
$$\frac{\operatorname{Re}\bigl((u-v)\overline{(w-v)}\bigr)}{\left|u-v\right|\left|w-v\right|} \;=\; \frac{\left|a\right|^2\cos\alpha}{\left|a\right|^2} \;=\; \cos\alpha .$$
Since $\alpha \in (0,\pi)$ by (0.1) and $\arccos$ is the inverse of $\cos|_{[0,\pi]}$, we get $\angle\,u\,v\,w = \alpha$. $\blacksquare$

(As a check, for $n=4$: $\omega = i$, $a = 1-i$, $b = -i(1-i) = -1-i$, and indeed $\angle = \pi/2 = \frac{(4-2)\pi}{4}$.)

## 6. The convex hull: $\partial C = P$ and $\operatorname{Int}P = \operatorname{int}C$

Recall $C = \operatorname{conv}\{z_0,\dots ,z_{n-1}\}$, a compact convex set.

**(6.1) $P \subseteq C$ and $P \cap \operatorname{int}C = \varnothing$; hence $P \subseteq \partial C$.**
Each $E_k$ is a segment with endpoints in $C$, so $E_k \subseteq C$ by convexity, giving $P \subseteq C$. By Corollary 2, $C \subseteq H_k$; since $\operatorname{int}C$ is an open subset of $H_k$, we get $\operatorname{int}C \subseteq \operatorname{int}H_k$, which is disjoint from $L_k \supseteq E_k$. As this holds for every $k$, $P\cap\operatorname{int}C = \varnothing$. Since $P \subseteq C$ and $C = \operatorname{int}C \sqcup \partial C$ for the closed set $C$, we get $P \subseteq \partial C$.

**Lemma 6 (extreme directions).** Let $u = e^{i\varphi}$ with $\varphi \in [0,2\pi)$ and $g(z) = \operatorname{Re}(z\bar u)$. Then the set
$$J \;=\; \{\, j \in \mathbb{N}_n : g(z_j) = \max_{0\le l\le n-1} g(z_l)\,\}$$
is either a singleton $\{j_0\}$ or a pair of cyclically consecutive indices $\{j_0,\ j_0+1 \bmod n\}$.

*Proof.* The $n$ intervals $\bigl[\frac{2j\pi}{n},\frac{2(j+1)\pi}{n}\bigr)$, $j \in \mathbb{N}_n$, partition $[0,2\pi)$; choose $j_0 \in \mathbb{N}_n$ with $\varphi \in \bigl[\frac{2j_0\pi}{n},\frac{2(j_0+1)\pi}{n}\bigr)$ and put $\psi = \varphi - \frac{2j_0\pi}{n} \in \bigl[0,\frac{2\pi}{n}\bigr)$.

For $j \in \mathbb{N}_n$ let $d \in \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ with $d \equiv j - j_0 \pmod n$. Then
$$g(z_j) \;=\; \operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e^{i(2j\pi/n - \varphi)}\Bigr) \;=\; \cos\Bigl(\frac{2j\pi}{n}-\varphi\Bigr) \;=\; \cos\Bigl(\frac{2d\pi}{n}-\psi\Bigr),$$
the last equality because the two arguments differ by an integer multiple of $2\pi$.

For $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ let $\delta(\theta) \in [0,\pi]$ denote the distance from $\theta$ to the nearest element of $2\pi\mathbb{Z}$; then $\cos\theta = \cos\delta(\theta)$, and since $\cos$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, $\cos\theta$ is a strictly decreasing function of $\delta(\theta)$. Note that $\delta(\theta) = \min(\theta, 2\pi - \theta)$ whenever $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.

* $d = 0$: the argument is $-\psi$ with $0 \le \psi < \frac{2\pi}{n} \le \frac{2\pi}{3} < \pi$, so $\delta = \psi$.
* $d = 1$: the argument is $\frac{2\pi}{n}-\psi \in \bigl(0,\frac{2\pi}{n}\bigr] \subseteq (0,\pi)$, so $\delta = \frac{2\pi}{n}-\psi$.

Hence
$$\min\bigl(\delta_0,\delta_1\bigr) \;=\; \min\Bigl(\psi,\ \frac{2\pi}{n}-\psi\Bigr) \;\le\; \frac{\pi}{n},$$
the last inequality because the minimum of two numbers does not exceed their arithmetic mean, here $\frac{\pi}{n}$.

* $2 \le d \le n-1$: put $\theta_d = \frac{2d\pi}{n}-\psi$. Then
$$\theta_d \;>\; \frac{2d\pi}{n}-\frac{2\pi}{n} \;=\;\frac{2(d-1)\pi}{n}\;\ge\;\frac{2\pi}{n}\;>\;0,\qquad
2\pi - \theta_d \;\ge\; 2\pi - \frac{2d\pi}{n} \;\ge\; 2\pi - \frac{2(n-1)\pi}{n} \;=\; \frac{2\pi}{n}\;>\;0 .$$
So $0 < \theta_d < 2\pi$ and $\delta(\theta_d) = \min(\theta_d, 2\pi-\theta_d) \ge \frac{2\pi}{n} > \frac{\pi}{n} \ge \min(\delta_0,\delta_1)$.

Therefore, for every $j$ with $j \not\equiv j_0, j_0+1 \pmod n$,
$$g(z_j) \;<\; \max\bigl(g(z_{j_0}),\,g(z_{j_0+1 \bmod n})\bigr) \;\le\; \max_l g(z_l),$$
so $J \subseteq \{j_0,\ j_0+1\bmod n\}$, which is the assertion. $\blacksquare$

**(6.2) $\partial C \subseteq P$; hence $\partial C = P$.**
Let $p \in \partial C$. Since $C$ is convex and $p$ is a boundary point, the supporting hyperplane theorem provides a non-zero linear functional attaining its maximum over $C$ at $p$; normalising, there is a unit $u = e^{i\varphi}$, $\varphi\in[0,2\pi)$, with
$$g(p) \;=\; \max_{x\in C} g(x) \;=:\; M, \qquad g(x) = \operatorname{Re}(x\bar u).$$
As $g$ is linear and $C$ is the convex hull of the finite set $\{z_0,\dots ,z_{n-1}\}$, we have $M = \max_{0\le l \le n-1} g(z_l)$. Write $p = \sum_{j} \lambda_j z_j$ with $\lambda_j \ge 0$, $\sum_j \lambda_j = 1$. Then $\sum_j \lambda_j g(z_j) = g(p) = M$ with every $g(z_j) \le M$, which forces $\lambda_j = 0$ whenever $g(z_j) < M$. Hence
$$p \in \operatorname{conv}\{z_j : j \in J\},\qquad J = \{j : g(z_j) = M\}.$$
By Lemma 6, either $J = \{j_0\}$, in which case $p = z_{j_0} \in P$; or $J = \{j_0, j_0+1 \bmod n\}$, in which case $p \in \operatorname{conv}\{z_{j_0},z_{j_0+1}\} = E_{j_0} \subseteq P$. Either way $p \in P$. Combined with (6.1), $\partial C = P$.

**(6.3) $\operatorname{Int}P = \operatorname{int}C$; in particular $P$ is convex.**
By Proposition 4, $C$ contains the non-degenerate triangle with vertices $z_0,z_1,z_2$, so $\operatorname{int}C \ne \varnothing$. Since $C$ is closed,
$$\mathbb{R}^2\setminus P \;=\; \mathbb{R}^2\setminus\partial C \;=\; \operatorname{int}C \;\sqcup\; \bigl(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C\bigr).$$
Now $\operatorname{int}C$ is non-empty, open, convex (hence connected) and bounded (as $C$ is bounded); and $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ is non-empty, open, unbounded and path-connected, as we now verify.

*$\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ is path-connected.* First, $0 \in C$: since $\omega\ne1$ (otherwise $(\ast)$ would give $n \mid 1$), the geometric sum formula gives $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}z_j = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\omega^{\,j} = \frac{\omega^{\,n}-1}{\omega-1} = 0$, so $0 = \frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}z_j$ is a convex combination of the $z_j$ and hence lies in $C$. Second, $C \subseteq \overline{\mathbb D} := \{x : \left|x\right| \le 1\}$, since each $z_j$ lies in the convex set $\overline{\mathbb D}$ by (1.2); hence the set
$$A \;=\; \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \left|x\right| \ge 2\}$$
is disjoint from $C$. Moreover $A$ is path-connected, being the image of the path-connected set $[2,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}$ under the continuous map $(r,\theta)\mapsto re^{i\theta}$. Now let $p \in \mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$; then $p \ne 0$ because $0 \in C$. For every $t\ge1$ we have $tp\notin C$: otherwise, since $0\in C$ and $C$ is convex, $p = \frac1t\,(tp) + \bigl(1-\frac1t\bigr)\cdot 0 \in C$, a contradiction. If $\left|p\right| \ge 2$ then $p\in A$ already; if $\left|p\right|<2$, the path $t\mapsto tp$ for $t\in[1, 2/\left|p\right|]$ (a genuine interval, as $2/\left|p\right|>1$) lies in $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ and joins $p$ to the point $\frac{2p}{\left|p\right|} \in A$. So every point of $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ is joined inside $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ to a point of $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$, and $A$ is path-connected; hence $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus C$ is path-connected.

Thus these two sets are precisely the two connected components of $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus P$, the bounded one being $\operatorname{int}C$. By definition, $\operatorname{Int}P = \operatorname{int}C$, which is convex. $\blacksquare$

## 7. $P$ is equiangular: every interior angle equals $\alpha$

Fix $k$ and keep the notation $v = z_{k+1}$, $a = z_k-v$, $b = z_{k+2}-v = e^{-i\alpha}a$ of Lemma 5. By Proposition 4, $a$ and $b$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$ (they are non-zero and non-parallel, since $z_k,v,z_{k+2}$ are not collinear). Hence every $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$ has a unique representation
$$x \;=\; v + \lambda a + \mu b,\qquad (\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb{R}^2,$$
and $(\lambda,\mu)\mapsto v+\lambda a + \mu b$ is a linear homeomorphism of $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $\mathbb{R}^2$. Set
$$\Gamma \;=\; \{\lambda a + \mu b : \lambda,\mu \ge 0\},$$
a closed convex cone; by the homeomorphism just mentioned, $\operatorname{int}\Gamma = \{\lambda a + \mu b : \lambda,\mu>0\}$.

**(7.1) $H_k \cap H_{k+1} = v + \Gamma$ and $\operatorname{int}H_k \cap \operatorname{int}H_{k+1} = v+\operatorname{int}\Gamma$.**
By Lemma 1, $f_k(z_k) = f_k(z_{k+1}) = c$ and $f_{k+1}(z_{k+1}) = f_{k+1}(z_{k+2}) = c$, while (using $n \ge 3$, so that $k+2\not\equiv k,k+1$ and $k \not\equiv k+1,k+2$ mod $n$)
$$f_k(z_{k+2}) < c,\qquad f_{k+1}(z_k) < c .$$
Put $\beta = c - f_k(z_{k+2}) > 0$ and $\gamma = c - f_{k+1}(z_k) > 0$. By linearity,
$$f_k(a) = f_k(z_k)-f_k(v) = 0,\quad f_k(b) = f_k(z_{k+2})-f_k(v) = -\beta,$$
$$f_{k+1}(a) = -\gamma,\quad f_{k+1}(b) = 0 .$$
Hence for $x = v+\lambda a+\mu b$,
$$f_k(x) = c - \mu\beta,\qquad f_{k+1}(x) = c - \lambda\gamma .$$
Therefore $x \in H_k \iff \mu \ge 0$, and $x \in H_{k+1} \iff \lambda\ge0$; likewise with strict inequalities for the interiors. This proves (7.1).

**(7.2) The set of "inward" directions at $v$.** Let
$$D \;=\; \{\,d : \left|d\right| = 1,\ v+td \in \operatorname{Int}P \text{ for all sufficiently small } t>0\,\}.$$
Then $D = \{d \in \operatorname{int}\Gamma : \left|d\right| = 1\}$.

*Proof.* ($\subseteq$) Let $d \in D$ and choose $t>0$ small with $v+td\in\operatorname{Int}P = \operatorname{int}C$ (by (6.3)). By Corollary 2, $C \subseteq H_k\cap H_{k+1}$, and $\operatorname{int}C$ is open, so $\operatorname{int}C \subseteq \operatorname{int}(H_k) \cap \operatorname{int}(H_{k+1}) = v + \operatorname{int}\Gamma$ by (7.1). Hence $td \in \operatorname{int}\Gamma$, and since $\operatorname{int}\Gamma$ is a cone stable under multiplication by $1/t>0$, $d \in \operatorname{int}\Gamma$.

($\supseteq$) Let $d = \lambda a + \mu b$ with $\lambda,\mu>0$ and $\left|d\right| = 1$. For $0 < t < \frac{1}{\lambda+\mu}$,
$$v + td \;=\; v + t\lambda(z_k - v) + t\mu(z_{k+2}-v) \;=\; \bigl(1-t\lambda-t\mu\bigr)v + t\lambda\,z_k + t\mu\, z_{k+2},$$
a combination of $v,z_k,z_{k+2}$ with coefficients that are all strictly positive and sum to $1$. Let $T = \operatorname{conv}\{v,z_k,z_{k+2}\}$; by Proposition 4 these three points are not collinear, so the map $(\lambda',\mu')\mapsto v+\lambda' a+\mu' b$ carries the triangle $\{\lambda',\mu'\ge0,\ \lambda'+\mu'\le1\}$ homeomorphically onto $T$ and its (open) interior $\{\lambda',\mu'>0,\ \lambda'+\mu'<1\}$ onto $\operatorname{int}T$. Hence $v+td \in \operatorname{int}T$. Finally $T \subseteq C$ (convex hull of three points of $C$), so $\operatorname{int}T \subseteq \operatorname{int}C = \operatorname{Int}P$. Thus $v + td \in \operatorname{Int}P$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$, i.e. $d \in D$. $\blacksquare$

**(7.3) The angular measure of $D$ is $\alpha$.**
Write $a = \left|a\right|\,e^{i\theta_0}$. Since $b = e^{-i\alpha}a$,
$$\Gamma \;=\; \{\lambda a + \mu e^{-i\alpha}a : \lambda,\mu\ge0\} \;=\; a\cdot\Gamma_0,\qquad \Gamma_0 := \{\lambda + \mu e^{-i\alpha} : \lambda,\mu\ge0\},$$
and multiplication by $a$ is the rotation by $\theta_0$ composed with the dilation by $\left|a\right|>0$, so it maps the set of unit vectors of $\Gamma_0$ bijectively and isometrically (as a map of the unit circle, rotation by $\theta_0$) onto the set of unit vectors of $\Gamma$. It therefore suffices to identify the unit vectors of $\Gamma_0$.

*Claim:* $\{w \in \Gamma_0 : \left|w\right| = 1\} = \{e^{-i\tau} : 0\le\tau\le\alpha\}$.
Indeed, let $w = \lambda + \mu e^{-i\alpha}$ with $\lambda,\mu\ge0$ and $\left|w\right| = 1$. Then
$$\operatorname{Im}(w) = -\mu\sin\alpha \le 0,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(we^{i\alpha}\bigr) = \lambda\sin\alpha \ge 0,$$
using $\sin\alpha>0$ (valid by (0.1)). Write $w = e^{i\sigma}$ with $\sigma\in(-\pi,\pi]$. From $\operatorname{Im}w = \sin\sigma\le0$ and $\sigma\in(-\pi,\pi]$ we get $\sigma\in(-\pi,0]$ or $\sigma=\pi$. The case $\sigma=\pi$ is impossible: it would give $w=-1$ and hence $\operatorname{Im}(we^{i\alpha}) = \operatorname{Im}(-e^{i\alpha}) = -\sin\alpha<0$, contradicting $\operatorname{Im}(we^{i\alpha})\ge0$. So $\sigma\in(-\pi,0]$, and then $\sigma+\alpha\in(-\pi+\alpha,\ \alpha]\subseteq(-\pi,\pi)$ since $0<\alpha<\pi$; now $\operatorname{Im}(we^{i\alpha}) = \sin(\sigma+\alpha)\ge0$ together with $\sigma+\alpha\in(-\pi,\pi)$ forces $\sigma+\alpha\ge0$. Hence $\sigma\in[-\alpha,0]$, i.e. $w = e^{-i\tau}$ with $\tau=-\sigma\in[0,\alpha]$. Conversely, for $\tau\in[0,\alpha]$ the identity
$$e^{-i\tau} \;=\; \frac{\sin(\alpha-\tau)}{\sin\alpha}\cdot 1 \;+\; \frac{\sin\tau}{\sin\alpha}\cdot e^{-i\alpha}$$
(which one verifies by expanding real and imaginary parts: $\sin(\alpha-\tau)+\sin\tau\cos\alpha = \sin\alpha\cos\tau$ and $-\sin\tau\sin\alpha = -\sin\alpha\sin\tau$) exhibits $e^{-i\tau}$ as such a combination with non-negative coefficients, since $0\le\tau\le\alpha<\pi$ gives $\sin\tau\ge0$ and $\sin(\alpha-\tau)\ge0$. This proves the claim.

Consequently the unit vectors of $\Gamma$ form the closed arc $\{e^{i(\theta_0-\tau)}: 0\le\tau\le\alpha\}$, of arclength $\alpha < \pi$. Since $\operatorname{int}\Gamma = \Gamma \setminus (\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}a \cup \mathbb{R}_{\ge0}b)$ (the two boundary rays correspond to $\mu = 0$ and $\lambda=0$), the unit vectors of $\operatorname{int}\Gamma$ form the corresponding open arc $\{e^{i(\theta_0-\tau)} : 0<\tau<\alpha\}$, again of arclength $\alpha$.

By (7.2), $D$ is this open arc, so the interior angle of $P$ at $z_{k+1}$ is $\alpha$.

Since $k$ was arbitrary, **every interior angle of $P$ equals $\alpha = \frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}$**, so $P$ is equiangular. $\blacksquare$

**Remark (consistency check).** The interior angles of a simple $n$-gon sum to $(n-2)\pi$. Here the sum is $n\cdot\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n} = (n-2)\pi$, as it must be. (Had some vertices been reflex, i.e. with interior angle $2\pi-\alpha$ instead of $\alpha$, the sum would have been $(n-2)\pi + \frac{4\pi m}{n}$ for $m \ge 1$ reflex vertices, which is $>(n-2)\pi$; so indeed no vertex is reflex, in agreement with §7.)

Combining §4 and §7: **$P$ is a regular $n$-sided polygon whose vertex set is exactly $U_n$**, with side length $2\sin\frac{\pi}{n}$ and interior angle $\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}$; it is convex by (6.3).

## 8. The circumscribed circle, and the vertex $\left(1,0\right)$

Let $S = \{z\in\mathbb{C}: \left|z\right| = 1\}$ be the unit circle, i.e. the circle of radius $1$ centred at $\left(0,0\right)$.

**(8.1) $S$ is circumscribed around $P$.** By (1.2) every vertex $z_j$ of $P$ satisfies $\left|z_j\right|=1$, i.e. lies on $S$. This proves assertion (1) of the Theorem apart from uniqueness.

**(8.2) $S$ is the *only* circle through the vertices of $P$.** Suppose the circle with centre $q$ and radius $r>0$ passes through $z_0,z_1,z_2$. From $\left|z_0-q\right| = \left|z_1-q\right|$ we get, squaring, $\left|z_0\right|^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}(z_0\bar q) = \left|z_1\right|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(z_1\bar q)$, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((z_1-z_0)\bar q\bigr) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\left|z_1\right|^2-\left|z_0\right|^2\bigr)$: a linear equation for $q$ with normal vector $z_1-z_0 \ne 0$, i.e. $q$ lies on a certain line $N_1$ (the perpendicular bisector of $[z_0,z_1]$). Similarly $q$ lies on the line $N_2$ determined by $z_1,z_2$, with normal vector $z_2-z_1$. By Proposition 4 the vectors $z_1-z_0$ and $z_2-z_1$ are not parallel (otherwise $z_0,z_1,z_2$ would be collinear), so $N_1$ and $N_2$ are non-parallel lines and meet in exactly one point; hence $q$ is uniquely determined, and then $r = \left|z_0-q\right|$ is determined too. Since $q=0$, $r=1$ is one solution, it is the only one. So $S$ is *the* circumscribed circle of $P$, proving (1).

**(8.3)** By (1.3), $z_0 = 1$ is a vertex of $P$, i.e. the point $\left(1,0\right)$ is one of the vertices. This proves (2).

## Conclusion

For every integer $n \ge 3$:

* $U_n = \{e^{2ik\pi/n} : k\in\mathbb{N}_n\}$ consists of $n$ distinct points of the complex plane (1.4) and is exactly the set of complex solutions of $z^n = 1$ (1.5);
* the closed polygonal curve $P = z_0z_1\cdots z_{n-1}z_0$ through them is a simple polygon with $n$ sides and vertex set $U_n$ (Propositions 3 and 4);
* $P$ is equilateral, each side having length $2\sin\frac\pi n$ (§4), and equiangular, each interior angle being $\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}$ (§7); hence $P$ is a **regular $n$-sided polygon**, and it is convex (6.3);
* $P$ is circumscribed by the unit circle centred at $\left(0,0\right)$, which is moreover the unique circle through its vertices (8.1)–(8.2);
* the point $\left(1,0\right)$ is one of its vertices (8.3).

$\blacksquare$
